def: A collective right of a First Nation to land it occupied before Crown sovereignty. Established by court declaration or agreement, and can only be transferred to the Crown.
Clear, unconditional agreement to all the terms of an offer, communicated to the offeror.
Admitting responsibility, for example by a partial payment on a fixed-sum claim or a written confirmation. Restarts both limitation clocks from that date.
Authority the principal has really given: express (in words), implied (needed to carry out the express authority) or usual/customary.
A FINTRAC fine for non-compliance: up to $100,000 per violation for individuals and $500,000 for entities, published publicly.
A fine of up to $100,000 per contravention that BCFSA can impose without a full hearing, set by category (A–F) in the Rules.
Each side presents its own case as strongly as it can, and a neutral judge decides. The judge only sees what the parties put forward.
A relationship in which one person (the agent) is authorized to act for another (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
The person authorized to represent and act for a principal.
A change by a life tenant that improves the property, such as adding a deck. Technically waste, but usually no damages are awarded.
The pull a first number (list price or first offer) exerts on the rest of a negotiation.
Announcing before the performance date that you won't perform. The other side can sue right away or wait.
Authority a third party reasonably believes an agent has because of the principal's conduct. Based on estoppel.
The party who brings an appeal.
The local official who decides whether a proposed subdivision is in the public interest and may require road or park dedication and services.
A private process where a neutral arbitrator hears both sides and makes a decision (an award) that is usually binding and final. Common in commercial leases.
Transferring the benefits (not the burdens) of a contract to someone else.
For Rules s.53: a licensee's spouse, a trust or estate they substantially benefit from, or a corporation or partnership where they or their spouse hold 5%+.
A licensee qualified to be a managing broker who works under the brokerage's managing broker.
A fund run by the LTSA that compensates people who lose land because of the Torrens system or land title office errors. A last resort.
A second offer accepted subject to the seller being released from the first contract.
The civil standard of proof: more likely than not. A tie means the plaintiff loses.
A strata development where land, rather than a building, is divided into strata lots. Roads and amenities are usually common property paid for by the owners.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you'll do if no deal is made. The source of negotiating power.
BC Financial Services Authority: the Crown agency that has regulated real estate licensees since 2021, along with mortgage brokers, credit unions, insurers and pensions.
BC Real Estate Association: the provincial association of the local boards. Provides standard forms, research, advocacy and the Professional Development Program.
For FINTRAC purposes, a person who directly or indirectly owns or controls 25% or more of an entity.
Failing to perform a contractual promise, including by refusing in advance (anticipatory breach) or making performance impossible.
The licensed business through which all real estate services are provided. Clients contract with the brokerage, not the individual licensee.
The model where the whole brokerage, and every licensee in it, is the client's agent. Now only for rental-only or strata-management-only brokerages.
A claim registered against land by an unpaid contractor, subcontractor or worker under the Builders Lien Act. Filed within 45 days of trigger dates; lasts 1 year unless enforced.
A set of restrictive covenants applied to every lot in a development sold by a common vendor, registered under LTA s.220. Common in bare land stratas.
The obligation to prove the case. In a civil case it's on the plaintiff.
A law passed by a municipality, such as a zoning or building bylaw.
The legal ability to make a binding contract. Minors and mentally incapable people have limited capacity.
The set of facts that gives someone the right to sue.
A registered warning by someone claiming an interest in land, blocking inconsistent dealings. Lapses after 2 months unless a lawsuit is started and a CPL registered.
"Let the buyer beware": buyers must inspect and take responsibility for what they find, subject to the seller's disclosure duties.
A notice on title that a lawsuit claiming an interest in the land has started. Formerly called lis pendens.
The official record of a parcel's fee simple owner, legal description and the charges registered against it.
Any registered interest in land less than a fee simple: mortgages, easements, covenants, leases, liens, judgments.
Personal property that isn't attached to land, such as furniture or free-standing equipment. The seller takes it unless the contract says otherwise.
BC's online tribunal for strata disputes (no monetary limit), small claims up to $5,000, motor vehicle claims up to $50,000, and co-op disputes.
Insurance that covers a claim only if it's reported during the policy term, as with the licensee E&O Indemnity Plan.
A separate binding promise made alongside the main contract, which can survive completion. Hard to prove.
A person appointed by the court to manage the affairs of an adult who can't manage them. The adult can no longer contract.
Law made by judges through written decisions, built up case by case since medieval England. In the broad sense it includes equity and is contrasted with statute law.
Both parties share the same mistaken belief about a fundamental fact, such as the property already being destroyed. The contract is void.
The parts of a strata development not within any strata lot, owned by all the owners as tenants in common.
Federal law against anti-competitive agreements (e.g. fixing commissions) and misleading advertising, enforced by the Competition Bureau.
The five-part PCMLTFA program every brokerage needs: compliance officer, written policies, documented risk assessment, written training, and a review every 2 years.
An essential term. A breach lets the innocent party end the contract and claim damages.
A "subject": an event that must happen before the contract becomes binding. Only a party for whose sole benefit it exists can waive it.
An event that ends obligations already in place (e.g. "if no occupancy permit by (date), this contract terminates").
Behaviour contrary to the public's best interests, or that undermines confidence in or discredits the real estate industry.
A substantial risk that your duty to a client will be affected by your own interests or a duty to someone else. Must be disclosed promptly, fully and in writing.
A discipline outcome agreed to by the licensee, based on their own proposal. It's published and can support a Special Compensation Fund claim.
Something of value each side gives in exchange for the other's promise. Courts don't review whether it's adequate.
The two roles under a Rules s.65 conflict agreement: the licensee keeps acting for the Continuing Client; the Released Client gets no further advice but keeps confidentiality.
An agreement between two or more people that creates a legal obligation to do, or not do, something.
The BC standard form contract between buyer and seller, created by BCREA and the Canadian Bar Association (BC Branch).
The brokerage working with the buyer, which usually shares in the listing brokerage's commission.
A share or membership in a cooperative association that comes with the right to occupy a unit.
A response that changes the terms of an offer. It rejects and ends the original offer.
An amount the court orders the losing party to pay the winner, set by a tariff. Covers only part of real legal fees, and is at the court's discretion.
An unconditional promise. Breaking it gives damages, but doesn't let the other party walk away.
Canadian Real Estate Association: the national organization that owns the REALTOR® and MLS® trademarks and the REALTOR® Code.
Condo and Strata Assignment Integrity Register: the provincial database of assignments of purchase agreements for residential strata lots in developments of 5+ lots, reported by developers.
Money a court orders one party to pay another as compensation for a wrong.
Fraudulent misrepresentation: a statement made knowing it's false or recklessly not caring whether it's true. Anyone can commit it.
A judgment against a party who failed to respond within the court's time limits. They lose without a hearing.
Good-faith money the buyer pays (usually within 24 hours of acceptance), held in trust by the brokerage as stakeholder. It isn't the consideration.
BC's model since June 2012: the brokerage names specific licensee(s) as the client's sole agents; the rest of the brokerage isn't the client's agent.
Under REDMA, land divided or to be divided into 5 or more units (2 or more for cooperative or shared interests), unless exempt.
A fine imposed after a discipline hearing or consent order: up to $500,000 for a brokerage or $250,000 for anyone else, per contravention.
The prescribed Rules s.53 form a licensee gives before any agreement when they or an associate will acquire or dispose of real estate.
A document a developer must file with BCFSA and give buyers before any agreement, setting out all material facts about a development.
The pre-trial process of exchanging evidence: questioning the other side under oath (examination for discovery) and exchanging all relevant documents.
To treat an earlier decision as not binding because a crucial fact is different.
On completion, the contract merges into the transfer, so most pre-completion promises can no longer be sued on (with exceptions such as fraud and surviving written warranties).
In an easement, the dominant tenement is the land that benefits; the servient tenement is the land that carries the burden.
Disclosure of Representation in Trading Services (Rules s.54): the prescribed form telling a consumer whether you'll represent them as a client.
The listing brokerage keeping the whole commission because the buyer has no agent. A conflict the s.57 disclosure exposes.
Representing clients with conflicting interests in the same trade. Banned in BC since 2018, except in remote, under-served areas where it's impracticable otherwise (Rules s.64).
A paper copy of title issued only on the owner's request since 1979. While it's out, transfers and mortgages can't be registered.
Pressure through threats (physical or economic) that forces someone into a contract. Makes it voidable.
Rules s.29: representatives and associate brokers must promptly tell their managing broker about possible misconduct in the brokerage.
Errors and omissions insurance: professional liability coverage for licensees' mistakes. Requires written notice of any circumstance that could lead to a claim, however weak.
A right to use a neighbour's land in a particular way (a right of way, a drain, light) for the benefit of your own land. Runs with the land if registered.
The brokerage whose efforts actually brought about the sale. Relevant to open listings and to sales after a listing expires.
A claim or burden registered against title, such as a mortgage, lien or judgment.
A power of attorney that continues after the donor loses capacity, and isn't subject to the 3-year limit for land.
A term saying the written contract is the whole deal. It can protect a seller against innocent misrepresentation but never against fraud, and never protects a licensee.
Flagrant or malicious destruction by a life tenant, such as arson. Not excused by "without impeachment for waste" unless expressly stated.
Principles of fairness developed by the courts of chancery to soften the rigid common law. Where equity and common law conflict, equity wins.
A mistake about the fundamental identity or character of what was sold. One of the exceptions to the doctrine of merger.
When a person dies with no will and no heirs, their land goes to the Crown.
A bundle of rights to hold land, rather than absolute ownership. Comes from the feudal system; the Crown still holds underlying title.
An estate measured by someone else's life, created when a life tenant sells their life estate. Ends when the original life tenant dies.
A rule that stops someone denying a state of affairs their own words or conduct led others to rely on.
Moral principles about right and wrong conduct. For licensees, following the spirit of the rules, not just the letter.
The usual BC listing: commission is payable on any sale during the term, even if the owner finds the buyer.
Enforcing a judgment by having the sheriff seize and sell the debtor's assets under a writ of execution.
The largest bundle of rights a private person can hold in land. The closest thing to ownership in Canada.
Someone in a position of trust who must put another's interests first: loyalty, avoiding conflicts, full disclosure, confidentiality and obeying lawful instructions.
The independent tribunal that hears appeals of BCFSA decisions. Appeals must be in writing within 30 days.
Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada: the federal agency that receives PCMLTFA reports, analyzes them and enforces compliance.
An insurance feature where no deductible applies if the insurer only paid defence costs and nothing went to the claimant.
Something attached to land or a building so that it's legally part of the real property. Stays with the property on a sale.
The prescribed Freehold Transfer used to transfer fee simple title in BC. The contract of purchase and sale itself isn't registered.
An outside event after the contract, not provided for, that makes performance fundamentally different. Ends the contract.
A court order directing someone who owes the debtor money (an employer or bank) to pay it into court instead. 70% of wages are exempt.
A court document confirming a will and the executor's authority to deal with the estate, including selling land.
Asking whether you'd be comfortable seeing your decision reported as a news headline. A quick ethics check.
Money kept back from a payment to protect against builders liens: 10% for 55 days, or 7% when buying a strata lot from the owner developer.
A 3-business-day right for buyers of most BC residential property to cancel an accepted offer, paying a 0.25% fee. Doesn't apply to REDMA sales.
Industrial, Commercial and Investment real estate: offices, retail, industrial, apartments, hotels, development land and businesses.
An agency created by conduct, e.g. by advising or negotiating for an unrepresented party, even without a written agreement.
The Torrens principle that the registered fee simple owner's title is conclusive and can't be defeated, subject to statutory exceptions. Doesn't extend to charges in BC.
A person under 19 in BC. Their contracts are unenforceable against them but enforceable by them (Infants Act).
An equitable court order telling someone to stop doing something. A mandatory injunction orders them to do something.
A licence that still exists but can't be used, for example when a licensee leaves their brokerage or their managing broker's licence is suspended.
An invitation for others to make offers, such as an ad, listing or display. Not an offer itself.
Co-ownership with a right of survivorship: when one owner dies, their interest passes to the surviving joint tenants. Needs the four unities of time, title, interest and possession.
The party who owes money under a court judgment, and the party who is owed it.
A court's review of a tribunal's decision, for unfair process (natural justice) or acting outside its jurisdiction.
The power of a court, tribunal or government over particular subjects, places or amounts.
Verifying and recording the identity of the people and entities you deal with, as required by the PCMLTFA.
Receiving $10,000 or more in cash in one transaction, or in several within 24 hours from or for the same person. Must be reported within 15 calendar days.
A hidden defect not discoverable by a reasonable inspection. A seller must disclose known latent defects that are dangerous or make the property uninhabitable.
A strata created on land leased for at least 50 years from a leasehold landlord (a government, certain First Nations or a university). Buyers get leases, not fee simple.
Permission to appeal. Required for the Supreme Court of Canada, which can refuse.
A court document appointing an administrator when there's no valid will. The administrator has no authority before it's granted.
Legally responsible.
Personal permission to do something on someone else's land. Not an interest in land, can't be registered and doesn't bind a buyer.
An estate lasting for the life of the life tenant. Registered as a charge. Afterwards the land goes to the remainderman or back to the reversioner.
The time limit for starting a lawsuit. In BC: 2 years from discovery, with a 15-year ultimate limit. Miss it and the right to sue is gone.
The pre-2018 arrangement where a licensee or brokerage represented both sides under an agreement limiting their duties. No longer allowed.
An amount agreed in the contract as compensation for breach. Enforced only if a genuine pre-estimate of loss; otherwise an unenforceable penalty.
The agreement between a seller and a brokerage: the brokerage markets the property, and the seller pays commission if a sale results. The buyer isn't a party.
Land Owner Transparency Act: BC law requiring disclosure of the individuals with indirect interests in land held through corporations, trusts or partnerships.
Land Owner Transparency Registry: the searchable registry created by LOTA. Separate from the title register and doesn't confirm ownership.
The Land Title and Survey Authority of BC, which has run the land title and survey systems since 2005.
The licensee responsible for running a brokerage: supervising licensees, trust accounts and records. Their licence category limits what the brokerage can do.

Under Rules s.59, a hidden defect that makes a property dangerous or unfit, would cost a great deal to fix, is subject to a local government notice, or lacks required permits. The seller's licensee must disclose it in writing before an agreement.
A process where a neutral mediator helps the parties reach their own settlement. The mediator doesn't decide anything.
Describing land by measurements, directions and landmarks. Used when part of an unsubdivided parcel is sold.
A false statement of fact that leads someone into a contract. The most common basis of claims against licensees.
The innocent party's duty to take reasonable steps to limit their losses after a breach.
Multiple Listing Service: the cooperative listing system run by real estate boards for their members. Not the same thing as realtor.ca.
Disguising the criminal origin of money or property so it appears legitimate. A Criminal Code offence, including when done recklessly.
The mortgagor is the borrower who grants the mortgage; the mortgagee is the lender who receives it.
The parties are at cross-purposes about the subject of the contract. Void if no reasonable reading of the contract can be found.
The LTSA's online service (formerly BC OnLine) for searching titles, plans and documents.
Basic fair-process rules, such as the right to be heard and an unbiased decision-maker.
Carelessness that causes harm. The plaintiff must prove a duty of care, a breach of the standard of care, and damage that isn't too remote.
A careless untrue statement by someone with special skill, reasonably relied on, causing loss (the five-part Queen v. Cognos test).
"No one can give what they don't have." At common law, a forged deed broke the chain of title for all later owners.
An arrangement where the licensee keeps whatever the sale price exceeds a set figure. Prohibited by Rules s.60.
"Not my deed." A defence that a signer didn't understand the basic nature of what they signed, making the document void.
The 1989 BCCA decision behind the CPS clauses that let transfers and mortgages register on lawyers' and notaries' undertakings.
A substantial and unreasonable interference with someone's use and enjoyment of their land, such as noise, smells or flooding.
"No goods." Marked on a writ of execution when the sheriff finds nothing to seize.
Under the Occupiers Liability Act, anyone in possession of premises or with responsibility for and control over them. There can be several, including a licensee at an open house.
A clear proposal that, if accepted, creates a binding contract.
A listing given to several brokerages at once. Only the brokerage that's the effective cause of the sale is paid, and the owner can sell commission-free.
A contract where the offeror receives separate consideration to keep an offer open for a set time.
The person a contract is being enforced against. Under LEA s.59, their signature on the writing is the one that matters.
Something done before a promise was made. It isn't valid consideration.
A defect discoverable by a reasonable inspection. Generally the buyer's responsibility.
Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act: the federal law requiring reporting entities to run compliance programs, verify identity, report and keep records.
A life tenant letting the property deteriorate by doing nothing. Generally not liable.
A corporation a licensee may use to receive their remuneration, mainly for tax planning. It doesn't shield the licensee from liability.
Parcel identifier: a permanent 9-digit number for each titled parcel. Found on the property tax notice or BC Assessment.
The three stages of money laundering: getting dirty money into the system, hiding its trail with complex transactions, and bringing it back as apparently legitimate wealth.
The party who sues. "Plaintiff" in BC Supreme Court; "claimant" in Small Claims Court.
The formal documents where each side states its case: notice of civil claim, response, reply, counterclaim. Their purpose is to narrow the issues.
A person holding (or who held) a prominent public position, or their family or close associates. Checked at the start of a relationship and on $100,000+ in cash or virtual currency.
A promise to do something, such as pay for maintenance. Generally doesn't run with the land, though an owner can become bound by conduct (Crystal Square).
A mailed acceptance takes effect when posted, not when received. It doesn't apply to revocations.
A document letting one person (the attorney) act for another (the donor). Ends on death, incapacity or bankruptcy; for land, generally usable for 3 years.
Buying a unit in a development before it's built or completed. Carries risks such as delays, changes and assignment restrictions.
An earlier court decision that later courts are expected to follow on similar facts.
Pressuring others to keep prices up, or punishing someone for low pricing. A civil matter under Competition Act s.76.
The person an agent acts for, such as the seller or buyer client of a brokerage.
Law governing disputes between individuals, such as contracts and torts. Also called civil law.
The rule that only the parties to a contract can enforce it or be bound by it.
Breaking RESA, its regulations or Rules, deceptive dealing, incompetence, not cooperating with an investigation and similar conduct under RESA s.35.
A right to enter someone's land and take something from it, such as timber, gravel or minerals. Can exist without a dominant tenement and can't be implied.
BCREA's form (since 1992) recording the seller's answers about the property. Not legally required and not a warranty unless incorporated into the contract.
BCREA's 2025 form for sellers who choose to disclose nothing beyond what the law requires. Replaced crossing out the PDS.
Law involving the state: criminal, tax and constitutional law.
"As much as is deserved": a reasonable payment for work when no price was agreed or a contract fails.
A principal approving, after the fact, an act done without authority, binding them as if it had been authorized from the start.
A non-profit that receives the interest on brokerage general trust accounts and funds land use, environmental and real estate education projects.
Under RESA, trading services, rental property management services or strata management services.
Detailed conduct and business rules made by BCFSA under RESA. Most discipline cases involve breaking one of them.
Two or more licensees at the same brokerage who present as one unit or regularly act for the same clients. Must register, can only provide trading services, and acts as one designated agent.
The STR threshold: a possibility of money laundering, based on facts a similarly trained person would also find suspicious. Lower than "reasonable grounds to believe".
Real Estate Development Marketing Act: the BC statute that controls how developers market development units, mainly through filed disclosure statements.
The person who receives the fee simple when a life estate ends, if it doesn't go back to the original grantor.
Any payment or benefit for a service, whether money or something else. Expecting to be paid is enough to trigger RESA licensing.
Leasing a rental for an owner, collecting rent or security deposits, and managing the property (payments, contracts, contractors, landlord–tenant matters).
A business with PCMLTFA obligations. Includes licensees and brokerages acting in the purchase or sale of real estate, but not pure rental or strata managers.
A document naming someone to help with personal and health decisions. One made after September 1, 2011 can't be used to sell real estate.
The most common licence level: a licensee who provides real estate services on behalf of their brokerage.
Real Estate Services Act: the BC statute that licenses and regulates real estate trading, rental property management and strata management, to protect the public.
Cancelling a contract so the parties go back to where they were. Under REDMA, buyers have a 7-day right that can't be waived.
Law-making power over matters the Constitution doesn't specifically assign. Held by the federal government.
Your bottom line in a negotiation, set in advance, beyond which you walk away.
A registered promise not to do something on your land (e.g. not build above 15 feet) for the benefit of neighbouring land. Must be negative in effect.
The original owner who gets the property back when a life estate they created ends.
Withdrawing an offer. Allowed any time before acceptance (even if the offer says "open until"), but only effective once communicated.
The feature of joint tenancy where a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants, outside the will.
A strata document setting each lot's share of the common property, generally used to split the strata's expenses.
A mark that can replace consideration, but only if the party knowingly adopts it. A corporate seal isn't the same thing.
Any undisclosed benefit an agent gets from acting for the principal. It must be handed over to the principal.
A covenant registered under LTA s.219 in favour of the province or a local government. Unlike common law restrictive covenants, it can be positive or negative.
The pre-1994 system in which a licensee working with a buyer was legally the seller's sub-agent.
Co-ownership of land with others, plus an agreement limiting each owner's use to a particular part.
Breaking up cash into many small deposits to avoid reporting thresholds. A placement technique.
Representing one party as a client in a trade, with no one else in that trade. The usual relationship under designated agency.
A fund that compensates people who lose money through a licensee's fraud, theft or intentional failure to account. Up to $200,000 per claimant and $1 million per brokerage.
An equitable remedy ordering a party to actually carry out a contract, such as transferring a property. Discretionary and can be lost through delay.
Someone holding money for two parties until conditions are met. A brokerage holds purchase deposits as stakeholder, not as either side's agent.
How carefully the law expects you to act. For licensees: what a competent real estate professional would do in the circumstances.
"Let the former decision stand." Courts follow earlier decisions on substantially the same facts.
A written law passed by Parliament, a provincial legislature or a municipal council. Also called legislation.
A right of way under LTA s.218 held by a government, utility or other authorized body. Unlike an ordinary easement, it needs no dominant tenement.
A non-physical feature that may affect a property's appeal, such as a past death or crime. No duty to disclose, but never lie if asked.
The part of a strata development owned individually, with its own title. Informally a "unit".
Collecting strata fees and levies and exercising powers a strata corporation delegates, such as paying bills, contracting and enforcing bylaws.
The plan deposited at the land title office that creates strata lots and common property.
Someone who buys property on behalf of another person to hide who really owns or pays for it. Also called a nominee.
Dividing land into two or more parcels. In BC it requires compliance with the Land Title Act and approval.
BCFSA's chief executive officer. Holds RESA's licensing, investigation and discipline powers and delegates most of them to BCFSA staff.
A report to FINTRAC, as soon as practicable, when there are reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering or terrorist financing. No dollar threshold.
Co-ownership where each owner holds a separate share (which can be unequal) that can be sold or left by will. No right of survivorship. Presumed in BC unless joint tenancy is clearly stated.
A term letting a seller with a backup offer require the first buyer to remove all subjects within a set time (typically 24–72 hours) or the contract ends.
Wording that makes deadlines essential, so missing one is a fundamental breach.
A right to use a property for recurring periods, such as one week a year, including fractional ownership.
Telling someone about a suspicious transaction report with intent to prejudice an investigation. Prohibited.
Insurance against title defects, fraud and issues like access, zoning and boundaries. A lender's policy protects only the lender.
A land registration system, from South Australia (1858), where title itself is registered and the register is the proof of ownership. Used in BC.
A private wrong, other than breach of contract, that injures someone and for which a court will award damages. Negligence is the most common.
A purchase, sale, lease or other acquisition or disposition of real estate, including assigning such a contract and any prospective trade.
Advising on price, making representations, finding property or buyers, showing, negotiating, presenting offers and receiving deposits for a trade in real estate.
Wrongfully entering, remaining on, or placing something on another person's land, including its airspace or subsurface.
A specialized decision-making body created by statute for one area of disputes. Not part of the court system, but its decisions can be reviewed by the courts.
A subject that depends entirely on a third party (e.g. a municipality). Waivable only under LEA s.54 by its sole beneficiary before the deadline.
An interest-bearing account at a BC savings institution where a brokerage holds other people's money, such as deposits, separate from its own funds.
A person or company holding property in their name for the benefit of someone else (the beneficiary).
The 15-year outer limit for most claims, usually running from the date of the act or omission, whether or not it was discovered.
A deal between unequal parties that is substantially unfair to the weaker one. The court may set it aside.
A written promise a licensee gives BCFSA to fix a minor problem and comply in future. Not published, but breaking it is misconduct.
A principal whose existence or identity the agent hides from the third party. The agent can then be personally liable on the contract.
Using a dominant relationship to push someone into a contract. Makes it voidable.
A valid contract that courts won't enforce because of a procedural problem, such as an oral contract for land.
One party is mistaken and the other knows it. The court may correct or set aside the contract.
Staff who may do administrative tasks such as filing, witnessing signatures and placing signs, but may not show property, host open houses, advise or negotiate.
A consumer a licensee helps in a limited way without being their agent. Must receive the DORTS and the Disclosure of Risks to Unrepresented Parties.
An order BCFSA can make without notice or a hearing, for example suspending a licence, when the public needs immediate protection.
Liability for someone else's wrong. A brokerage is liable for its licensees' acts in the ordinary course of their work, even fraud.
A contract treated as never having existed, for example due to common mistake or illegality.
A document that looks valid but has no legal effect: a forged deed, one for an illegal purpose, or one subject to non est factum.
A valid contract that one party may choose to cancel, for example after misrepresentation, duress or undue influence.
A life tenant actively damaging or destroying part of the property, such as demolishing a garage. Liable.
A minor term. A breach gives damages only; the contract continues.
An agent's implied promise to third parties that they have the authority they're using. Breaching it makes the agent personally liable.
Provincial permission to use surface or groundwater under the Water Sustainability Act. Not recorded in the land title office; passes to a buyer with any unpaid fees.
